articles.title: Build a Small Model, Understand Large Models
articles.goal: Understand why model mechanisms matter and which development and verification skills this course builds.
articles.short_summary: When a model gets an answer wrong, should you inspect the input, generation, or training? Start with a model you can calculate by hand and build a basis for those decisions.

articles.title: Before We Begin | Test the Finished Model, Then Build It from Scratch
articles.goal: Distinguish training from generation and find the starting point for the course.
articles.short_summary: The same opening produces nonsense from random weights and a meaningful continuation after training. Asking a question fails again. Inspect these changes, then run the first numerical example.

articles.title: 01 | Neurons: What Does a Model Calculate Before It Writes the Next Character?
articles.goal: Explain the roles of inputs, parameters, and activation.
articles.short_summary: How do two inputs, two weights, and one bias produce 4? Then use an impossible target to see why activation functions are needed.

articles.title: 02 | Vectors and Matrices: Do Two Outputs Require Two Copies of the Code?
articles.goal: Explain input, parameter, and output shapes axis by axis.
articles.short_summary: Arrange two parameter groups in a table to calculate two outputs at once. Add another input sample and see which numbers need to be duplicated and which parameters remain shared.

articles.title: 03 | Nonlinearity: Why Can Multiply-and-Add Not Express Four Simple Rules?
articles.goal: Explain the difference between stacking layers and adding nonlinearity.
articles.short_summary: The first three rules can all be satisfied, but the fourth must fail. Follow the four inputs to see why another layer is not enough and what ReLU changes.

articles.title: 04 | Gradients: Why Can an Update in the Right Direction Make Things Worse?
articles.goal: Distinguish the local direction given by a gradient from the actual update step size.
articles.short_summary: With the same negative gradient, a small update reduces error while a large one overshoots the target. Use a reproducible curve to understand local direction and learning rate.

articles.title: 05 | Backpropagation: Must We Test All 9 Parameters One by One?
articles.goal: Calculate one backward path by hand and explain how branch contributions combine before parameters are updated together.
articles.short_summary: The forward pass produces −1 and a loss of 4. Trace one path backward: why does a weight whose value is 0 have a gradient of −8?

articles.title: 06 | The Training Loop: What Happens to Four Predictions After 500 Updates?
articles.goal: Write one training iteration, explain gradient clearing, and identify incorrect comparisons caused by broadcasting.
articles.short_summary: Have the same small network repeatedly run forward, calculate loss, backpropagate, and update. Observe 500 updates, then uncover a shape error that leaves a nonzero loss even when every prediction is correct.

articles.title: 07 | Embedding: How Does Text Become a Network Input?
articles.goal: Distinguish character IDs, embedding vectors, and the three tensor axes.
articles.short_summary: The ID 44 is not the meaning of “欢”. Give characters addresses, then retrieve vector rows from a trainable table to connect text to numerical computation.

articles.title: 08 | Softmax: How Do Scores Become Next-Character Probabilities?
articles.goal: Explain candidate scores, relative competition, and normalization.
articles.short_summary: The score for “红” stays the same, but its probability decreases. Put red, yellow, and green in the same competition and calculate exponentials and normalization step by step.

articles.title: 09 | Training Targets: How Does a Sentence Become a Learnable Task?
articles.goal: Construct shifted targets and explain average loss over valid positions.
articles.short_summary: The training answers are already in the original sentence: shift inputs and targets by one position. Then see how loss scores predictions and why padding must be excluded from the average.

articles.title: 10 | Attention: How Does Predicting the Next Character Read Earlier Text?
articles.goal: Calculate one attention row and distinguish reading proportions from the content being read.
articles.short_summary: Putting preceding text in an array does not necessarily connect it to the current prediction. First read three positions in chosen proportions, then see how Q and K calculate those proportions.

articles.title: 11 | Causal Masks: Why Is Parallel Training Not Peeking at the Answer?
articles.goal: Explain causal visibility and the correct placement of the mask.
articles.short_summary: The future answer is already in memory. Why can the current position still not read it? Draw the permitted connections, then exclude forbidden scores before normalization.

articles.title: 12 | Multi-Head Attention: Where Does Each Head Read?
articles.goal: Explain head splitting, independent attention weights, and merging, and identify incorrect axes even when shapes match.
articles.short_summary: One sentence can be read in several ways. Explore the limits of one set of weights, move numbered cells into separate heads, aggregate independently, and merge by position.

articles.title: 13 | RoPE: How Does the Model Know the Order?
articles.goal: Connect the two-dimensional rotation formula to relative positions and Q/K dot products.
articles.short_summary: Reordering content can leave an attention result unchanged. Use two rotating arrows to connect coordinates, radians, and relative position step by step.

articles.title: 14 | SwiGLU: What Happens After Reading the Prefix?
articles.goal: Explain input-dependent gating and positionwise processing.
articles.short_summary: How can two conditions jointly affect one output? Compute multipliers from the current input and observe sign changes, zeroing, shrinking, and amplification.

articles.title: 15 | Residual Connections and RMSNorm: Why Keep a Direct Path?
articles.goal: Assemble head splitting, rotation, and causal aggregation into an attention component, then add residual connections and a Pre-Norm model block.
articles.short_summary: If a new branch returns zero, does the earlier information survive? See what the direct path preserves, then adjust the scale of the values entering the branch.

articles.title: 16 | The Complete Model: Follow the Character “欢” Through Every Step
articles.goal: Assemble the complete model and distinguish representations, parameters, and vocabulary scores.
articles.short_summary: Start with 14 IDs and follow the row for “欢”: how do its 64 representation values change, and how do they finally produce 79 candidate scores?

articles.title: 17 | Pretraining: Why Can New Questions Get Worse as Training Questions Improve?
articles.goal: Complete pretraining and use differences in the data to explain changes in evaluation results.
articles.short_summary: Training loss keeps falling while held-out loss rises. Inspect how the two sets differ, then follow one batch through an actual parameter update.

articles.title: 18 | Generation: How Many Choices Does One Sentence Take?
articles.goal: Write a generation loop and explain random selection and stopping conditions.
articles.short_summary: Six visible characters require seven choices. Feed each selected character back into the input and trace the growing prefix, sampling, and the final EOS.

articles.title: 19 | Supervised Fine-Tuning: Why Can It Continue Text but Still Fail to Answer?
articles.goal: Build answer supervision and diagnose fine-tuning tradeoffs with fixed comparisons across three methods and three seeds.
articles.short_summary: A model learns to answer questions while old capabilities may degrade. Align answer labels, then compare learning rates and mixed training on fixed evaluation tasks to measure both gains and costs.

articles.title: 20 | The Full Workflow: Connect Pretraining, Fine-Tuning, and Generation
articles.topic: The full workflow and checks of the principles
articles.goal: Independently complete a transfer experiment covering data, vocabulary, model construction, training, and reloading, and explain both successes and failures.
articles.short_summary: Reconnect inputs, labels, parameters, and saved weights across the full workflow. Swap facts and retrain, then add Xiaotang and tangerines yourself to verify your implementation and explain missing words in a new sentence pattern.

articles.title: Closing Thoughts | You Can Now Explain Those “Red Apples”
articles.goal: Bring together what you learned and choose a concrete, testable next experiment.
articles.short_summary: Revisit the opening example, trace the difference between training and generation, and plan a next step using your own data, a new task, or a publicly available model.
